children: By Nate Raymond

A US appeals court concluded on Tuesday that a federal law barring felons from owning guns can only be constitutionally applied when a person's prior conviction involved violence or threats suggesting a risk of firearms misuse.

The full Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals in a pair of decisions ruled that in such cases, the primary federal law used to keep guns out of felons' hands does not violate the US Constitution's Second Amendment.

The court, which now has a conservative majority following recent appointments by Republican President Donald Trump, said the law could be used to disarm a man convicted in a carjacking case but not against another man whose conviction stemmed from a DUI conviction.

The decisions came in the latest in a series of court cases grappling with whether modern firearms restrictions remain valid after ​the Supreme Court handed down a landmark Second Amendment ruling in 2022 that expanded gun rights.

The 6-3 conservative majority's decision, New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. ​Bruen, held that modern gun restrictions must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation."

One of the cases before the 3rd Circuit concerned James Bost, who had pleaded guilty to terroristic threats and criminal conspiracy charges in Pennsylvania state court arising out of a 2002 carjacking.

When he was later indicted for possessing a gun despite his convictions, he moved to dismiss the case, arguing the ban, which dates to the 1960s, ran afoul of his right to keep and bear arms under the Second Amendment.

But US Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas, writing for the majority in Bost's case, said individuals convicted of crimes like Bost's that demonstrate a risk of physical violence from misusing guns may presumptively be disarmed based on their convictions alone.
"The right to keep and bear arms has limits, and this is one: Those who pose a risk of physical violence from misusing guns can be disarmed before that risk becomes a reality,"
Bibas, a Trump appointee, for a 12-2 court.
But the 3rd Circuit

along ideological lines in the separate case of Edward Williams, who had two convictions for driving under the influence of alcohol in the early 2000s, including one that triggered the federal ban, which covers offenses that are punishable by at least one year in prison.

Williams had been sentenced to 90 days to two years, which he served in home confinement. Upon learning the conviction barred him from owning guns, he sued in order to secure a declaration that the law was unconstitutional as applied to his offense.

In a majority decision joined only by Republican-appointed judges, Trump-appointed US Circuit Judge Paul Matey agreed as he rejected the Justice Department's contention that historical laws targeting "habitual drunkards" showed the law fell within the nation's tradition of firearms regulation.
Matey called Williams "a peaceable citizen, capable of bearing arms consistent with the design of the Second Amendment."

"And with that rehabilitation comes restoration of the civic privileges guaranteed to citizens by the Constitution, and the freedom to again exercise the natural right of armed defense against threats and tyranny," he wrote.

The six dissenting judges were all appointed by Democratic presidents, including US Circuit Judge Arianna Freeman, who said she parted ways "from the majority opinion when it says a prior conviction is disarming on its face only if it involved violence or threats."

While convictions that require violence or threats certainly qualify, the judge said, so do other offenses, including for drunk driving, "that show a person poses a credible threat to the physical safety of others."

Joshua Prince, a lawyer for Williams, welcomed the ruling, which he said made clear "there does not exist any historical tradition of stripping individuals with non-violent convictions of their Second Amendment rights and whom do not pose a threat to the public in possession of a firearm."
The cases in the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals are United States v Bost, No. 24-1719, and Williams v Attorney General, No. 24-1091.
For the United States in Bost: Donovan Cocas of the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Pennsylvania
For the United States in Williams: Vivek Suri of the US Department of Justice
For Bost: Jasmine Sola of the Federal Public Defender's Office for the Western District of Pennsylvania
For Williams: Joshua Prince of Prince Law Offices
